content.title: Joining clauses without comma splices
content.instructions: Join the sentences into ONE correctly punctuated sentence using the punctuation mark, linker or structure given. Change or remove words where necessary and write the complete new sentence.

items.prompt: Canada had the highest recycling rate in 2020. Greece had the lowest. Use: a semicolon
accepted_answers: Canada had the highest recycling rate in 2020; Greece had the lowest.
items.model_answer: Canada had the highest recycling rate in 2020; Greece had the lowest.
items.explanation: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a linker, which works well for balanced Task 1 contrasts. The word after a semicolon is not capitalised unless it is a proper noun (like 'Greece').

items.prompt: Air travel has become much cheaper. More people are taking short holidays abroad. Use: 'as a result'
accepted_answers: Air travel has become much cheaper; as a result, more people are taking short holidays abroad.
items.model_answer: Air travel has become much cheaper; as a result, more people are taking short holidays abroad.
items.explanation: Adverbial linkers (as a result, therefore, consequently, however) are not conjunctions. To join two clauses with one in a single sentence, put a semicolon before the linker and a comma after it.

items.prompt: Housing in the city centre is extremely expensive. Many key workers commute from surrounding towns. Use: 'so'
accepted_answers: Housing in the city centre is extremely expensive, so many key workers commute from surrounding towns.
items.model_answer: Housing in the city centre is extremely expensive, so many key workers commute from surrounding towns.
items.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, so, or, yet) can join two independent clauses. Put a comma before the conjunction when the two clauses have different subjects, as here.

items.prompt: The Amazon rainforest is home to around 10% of the world's known species. It is being destroyed at an alarming rate. Use: ', which …,'
accepted_answers: The Amazon rainforest, which is home to around 10% of the world's known species, is being destroyed at an alarming rate.
items.model_answer: The Amazon rainforest, which is home to around 10% of the world's known species, is being destroyed at an alarming rate.
items.explanation: The extra information becomes a non-defining relative clause placed inside the main clause and enclosed by two commas. Because 'the Amazon rainforest' is already identified, the commas are compulsory and 'that' cannot replace 'which'.

items.prompt: Cities invest in cycling infrastructure. Car use usually falls significantly. Use: 'When'
accepted_answers: When cities invest in cycling infrastructure, car use usually falls significantly.
Car use usually falls significantly when cities invest in cycling infrastructure.
items.model_answer: When cities invest in cycling infrastructure, car use usually falls significantly.
items.explanation: A subordinate clause at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma. If the 'when' clause comes second, no comma is needed.

items.prompt: My grandfather worked as a farmer for forty years. He has seen enormous changes in agriculture. Use: ', who …,'
accepted_answers: My grandfather, who worked as a farmer for forty years, has seen enormous changes in agriculture.
items.model_answer: My grandfather, who worked as a farmer for forty years, has seen enormous changes in agriculture.
items.explanation: 'My grandfather' refers to one specific person, so the added information is non-defining and needs a comma on both sides. This is also a natural way to add detail to a Speaking Part 2 or 3 answer.

items.prompt: The government has two options. It can raise taxes or cut public spending. Use: a colon
accepted_answers: The government has two options: it can raise taxes or cut public spending.
The government has two options: raising taxes or cutting public spending.
The government has two options: to raise taxes or to cut public spending.
items.model_answer: The government has two options: it can raise taxes or cut public spending.
items.explanation: A colon introduces an explanation or list that completes what the first clause promises ('two options'). The part before the colon must be a complete clause, and in British English the word after the colon is normally lower case.

items.prompt: The weather was poor. The festival attracted a record number of visitors. Use: 'Despite'
accepted_answers: Despite the poor weather, the festival attracted a record number of visitors.
items.model_answer: Despite the poor weather, the festival attracted a record number of visitors.
items.explanation: An introductory prepositional phrase (Despite…, According to the chart…, In 2020…) is normally followed by a comma. Remember that 'despite' takes a noun phrase ('the poor weather'), not a clause.

items.prompt: London is the capital of the United Kingdom. It attracts millions of international tourists every year. Use: an appositive ('London, …,')
accepted_answers: London, the capital of the United Kingdom, attracts millions of international tourists every year.
items.model_answer: London, the capital of the United Kingdom, attracts millions of international tourists every year.
items.explanation: An appositive is a noun phrase that renames the noun before it. When it adds non-essential information, it is enclosed by two commas, like a non-defining relative clause without 'which is'.

items.prompt: Exports of tea rose by 10%. Exports of coffee fell by 5%. Use: 'while'
accepted_answers: Exports of tea rose by 10%, while exports of coffee fell by 5%.
Exports of tea rose by 10%, whereas exports of coffee fell by 5%.
items.model_answer: Exports of tea rose by 10%, while exports of coffee fell by 5%.
items.explanation: 'While' (or 'whereas') contrasts two parallel facts. Put a comma before 'while' when it means 'whereas', so that it is not read as 'during the time that'.
